clusters.name: Teodor's death, 1978–1979
clusters.reason: Around your grandfather Teodor's collapse and death in January 1978, within the next year: your grandmother Delphine stopped cooking and went to your mother's every evening; your father took night shifts and distanced from your mother; your uncle Anton drank at lunch and was warned at work, then separated from Celeste; your mother's anxiety rose over them; and your brother Callum had ear infections through the winter. These shifts pile up from February through May 1979, when your grandmother took a job at the library and began functioning better. The period holds the family's reactions across the generations to the loss.

clusters.name: Odette's bed rest, 1984
clusters.reason: Around your mother being ordered to bed for the rest of her pregnancy in March 1984, within four months: your grandmother Hazel came every morning to keep house and overfunctioned; your father argued with her over how she kept it; your brother Callum stammered again after being free of it; and you would not sleep unless your father sat by the bed, though the month is uncertain. All four shifts fall between March and July, and your sister Ines was born in September. The period holds the family's response to your mother's loss of functioning.

clusters.name: Hazel's Parkinson's diagnosis, 1986–1996
clusters.reason: Around your grandmother Hazel's diagnosis with Parkinson's disease in September 1986, over the next ten years: your grandfather Ambrose took over her cooking and all her appointments and overfunctioned; your father phoned his father every night for news and his anxiety rose; Hazel had a fall and her functioning dropped, then rose briefly on new medicine, then dropped again; your father and uncle Lyle argued over who should help their parents; your grandfather developed chest pains; Hazel could no longer dress herself; your mother overfunctioned, taking her to the clinic twice a week; your aunt Mavis came to stay one week in four to nurse her sister; your father drank most evenings; your aunt Pearl had panic spells at the wheel; Hazel had a good summer in her chair, then could no longer stand and needed a nurse every morning; your grandfather gave up his workshop and hardly left her side; your father fought with your mother over his evenings at his parents' house. The shifts build across the decade, each step bringing a new crisis, with no long quiet between them until Hazel moved into the nursing home in June 1997.

clusters.name: Callum leaving home, 1999–2000
clusters.reason: Around your brother Callum leaving home for work up north in May 1999, within the following months: your father and Callum argued most nights over his plans; your mother could not settle at the thought of him so far away and her anxiety rose; your father missed days at work and sat up late in the garage; your sister Ines skipped school most of that autumn; your mother took Ines with her everywhere, even to work; and by August 2000 Ines was back at school full days and passed her exams. The period holds your father's and mother's and sister's responses to Callum's departure.

clusters.name: Hazel's death, 2003
clusters.reason: Around your grandmother Hazel's death in January 2003, within the following months: you could not sleep more than a few hours a night; you stopped going in to the bookshop and were let go in May; you dreaded buses and crowded shops and went out only after dark; and in November you took a job at the garden centre and slept through the night again. All your shifts fall between February and August, and your functioning returned in November. The period holds your own response to her death, and no one else's shifts show in these months.
